paras: The attempted lynching of John Wood took place at Yates Center, Woodson County, Kansas, on the night of May 27-28, 1903, when a mob of about 300 made three attempts on the county jail to seize Wood, a Black man charged with assaulting a farmer's wife, Mrs. Lind. Officers held off the mob and took Wood to Wichita; he was later convicted. The Topeka Plaindealer, a Black weekly, used the episode to explain Kansas's new anti-lynching law.

According to the Wichita Daily Eagle, Wood had come to Yates Center about two years earlier and was "the only negro in the town" or the county; the Topeka State Journal said he had worked on the Lind farm. On Tuesday, May 26, he was accused of luring Mrs. Lind into a buggy on a false errand and assaulting her in timber near town. Officers found him in a smoke house where he boarded, and he made no resistance.

On Wednesday there was "considerable bitter talk" against Wood, and he was bound over to the district court at a preliminary hearing. At dusk, the Eagle reported, Mrs. Lind's eldest son began agitating for a lynching and a mob formed. Sheriff Patterson gathered deputies and volunteers, all armed.

The mob came to the jail with a heavy timber from the railroad yards to use as a battering ram, but the sheriff and County Attorney Florence met it at the door and talked it away. It returned twice more, the third time smaller but "more determined than ever," and was again held back. A Yates Center dispatch credited Florence and ex-Senator Lamb with counseling moderation and said Patterson, armed with a Winchester, made "an impassioned speech to the mob."

Close to 1 a.m., while the mob regrouped, Patterson, Undersheriff Bartlett and the county attorney slipped the shackled prisoner into a carriage. They drove eighteen miles to Toronto, caught a Missouri Pacific train, and lodged Wood in the Sedgwick County jail at Wichita.

After a two-day trial at Yates Center in November 1903, a jury found Wood guilty, and Judge Fouse sentenced him to five years in the penitentiary at Lansing. No report of any arrest of mob members appears in the coverage.

Kansas white papers stated the accusation as fact: the State Journal's first report was headed "MAY BE LYNCHED. Negro Assaults Farmer's Wife" and called Wood "the brute," and the Eagle ran the militia dispatch under "Negro Rapist Be Protected." The Eagle's local account, "SPENT AWFUL NIGHT," praised the guards as "duty bound to protect" the prisoner while calling Wood "rather a vicious looking citizen."

The militia dispatch ran as a short wire item in the Omaha Daily Bee, the Saint Paul Globe and the Norfolk Weekly News-Journal on May 28 and 29. The Walla Walla Evening Statesman headlined "KANSAS FARMERS Attempt To Lynch a Negro WHO OUTRAGED PRETTY MRS. LIND," and the Durango Semi-Weekly Herald carried the Yates Center dispatch on June 1.

The Topeka Plaindealer ran the story on June 5 under "IT IS A CURE FOR LYNCHING," crediting the text to the State Journal. It described Wood as held "on the charge of assaulting a white woman" and explained that the new law made lynchers punishable as for first-degree murder and required a sheriff to notify the governor when a prisoner was in danger. It added that the law did not punish failed attempts.

The papers gave the accused as John Wood, John Woods or J. M. Woods and the complainant as Mrs. J. C., J. G., John or Julia Lind. The State Journal placed the attack Tuesday afternoon and the Eagle's dispatch about 10 p.m.; the November report said "last June."

Wire reports said the mob battered down the jail door with a telephone pole, while the Eagle, drawing on the officers, said it was talked away at the door. The Eagle said the sheriff meant to avoid force, whereas the Plaindealer's text said officers faced the mob with drawn revolvers and threatened to shoot. A Topeka dispatch said the sheriff telegraphed the governor for militia, the Plaindealer said he tried to telephone, and the Yates Center dispatch said "No request for troops was made."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of John Wood
bases: A mob of about 300 made three attempts to take Wood from the Yates Center jail to lynch him and was held off by officers, an attempted lynching (A7, A6, A11, A12).

A local Wichita account (A7), separate Yates Center and Topeka dispatches (A1, A2, A6, A10), the Black press (A11) and the November trial report (A12) agree that a mob tried to lynch Wood at the jail and that he was removed to Wichita.

accounts.label: Wichita Daily Eagle local account (officers' side)
accounts.gist: The complainant's eldest son raised a mob that came three times to the jail with a timber; the sheriff and county attorney talked it down, and near 1 a.m. the officers slipped Wood out by carriage to Toronto and by train to Wichita.

accounts.label: Yates Center wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Three hundred men battered down the jail door with a telephone pole but were stopped by the county attorney, ex-Senator Lamb and the armed sheriff, and dispersed at midnight; no request for troops was made.

accounts.label: Topeka militia wire
accounts.gist: The sheriff telegraphed the governor for a company of militia, saying he could not protect Woods much longer from a mob surrounding the jail.

accounts.label: Topeka Plaindealer (State Journal text)
accounts.gist: A mob of 300 with a plank was faced by officers with drawn revolvers and kept approaching until 1 a.m., when the officers took Woods to Wichita; the sheriff tried to telephone the governor.

framing.detail: The Topeka State Journal headlined 'MAY BE LYNCHED. Negro Assaults Farmer's Wife' and called Wood 'the brute', stating the accusation as fact while reporting the lynching threat.
The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the Topeka militia wire under 'Sheriff at Yates Center Asks That Negro Rapist Be Protected.'

The Eagle's local account praised the guards as 'duty bound to protect' the prisoner and called the night 'a most terrible experience' for the officers, but stated the assault as fact and called Wood 'rather a vicious looking citizen.'
Out-of-state papers ran short wire items, the Walla Walla Evening Statesman under 'KANSAS FARMERS Attempt To Lynch a Negro WHO OUTRAGED PRETTY MRS. LIND.'
The State Journal's November item 'A Negro Sent to Lansing' reported the verdict and recalled the three lynching attempts.
The Topeka Plaindealer headlined 'IT IS A CURE FOR LYNCHING', used 'on the charge of' for the accusation, and turned the story into an explanation of the new anti-lynching law.
